name: Vestibular Neuritis
preview_text: The sudden spinning of vestibular neuritis isn't a single disease in TCM - it's a sign that phlegm and wind are blocking the head, or that your deepest reserves are depleted. The r...
conventional_description:
Vestibular neuritis is an inflammation of the vestibular nerve, which connects the inner ear to the brain and helps control balance. It typically causes sudden, severe vertigo - a spinning sensation that worsens with head movement - along with nausea, vomiting, and unsteadiness, but usually no hearing loss or tinnitus. Most cases are thought to be triggered by a viral infection, and symptoms can last from a few days to several weeks, with gradual recovery.
Diagnosis is based on a physical exam and history, often including the head impulse test or caloric testing. While the acute phase is debilitating, conventional medicine focuses on symptom relief and vestibular rehabilitation exercises to retrain the brain's balance system.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment includes vestibular suppressants like meclizine or diazepam to reduce spinning sensations, and anti-nausea medications. Short courses of corticosteroids may be prescribed to reduce nerve inflammation. Once the severe vertigo subsides, vestibular rehabilitation therapy (VRT) - a series of customized exercises - helps the brain compensate for the damaged nerve signals and restore balance.
tcm_understanding: TCM views vestibular neuritis as a disorder of the head's clear orifices, caused by internal wind, phlegm, or fire rising upward or by deficiencies that fail to nourish the brain and inner ear. It is not a single disease but a constellation of patterns: Wind-Phlegm obstructing the head, Liver Yang Rising, Kidney Essence Deficiency, Qi and Blood Deficiency, Blood Stagnation, and Spleen Qi Sinking. The specific pattern is identified by the quality of vertigo, accompanying symptoms, and tongue and pulse signs. Treatment aims to restore balance by addressing the root pattern, not just suppressing the spinning sensation.
classical_translation: "When wind-phlegm harasses upward, there is dizziness and deafness."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking you to describe the vertigo: does it feel like the room is spinning, or more like a heavy, foggy sensation? The quality of the dizziness, along with what triggers it and what other symptoms accompany it, provides the first clues that point toward one of several underlying patterns.
If the vertigo comes with a heavy head, chest tightness, nausea, and a lot of phlegm, Wind-Phlegm is likely. The tongue often shows a thick, greasy white coating, and the pulse feels slippery and wiry. This pattern is very common after eating rich, damp-producing foods.
When vertigo strikes suddenly with irritability, a red face, bitter taste, and a roaring tinnitus, Liver Yang Rising is suspected. The tongue is red with a thin yellow coat, and the pulse is wiry and rapid. Anger or stress often brings it on.
Chronic vertigo with a soft, buzzing tinnitus, weak lower back and knees, and poor memory points to Kidney Essence Deficiency. The tongue looks pale with little coating, and the pulse is deep and thin. This pattern reflects a deeper, long-term depletion.
If the dizziness worsens with tiredness and is paired with a pale face, heart palpitations, and poor appetite, Qi and Blood Deficiency is the likely picture. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is thin and weak, especially after exertion.
Vertigo accompanied by a fixed, stabbing headache, a dark complexion, and a history of head injury suggests Blood Stagnation. The tongue may appear dark purple with stasis spots, and the pulse feels choppy. This pattern is less common but important to identify.
When dizziness is coupled with extreme fatigue, poor appetite, loose stools, and a dragging sensation, Spleen Qi Sinking is considered. The tongue is pale with a thin coat, and the pulse is weak. This pattern indicates that the body's uplifting energy is failing to reach the head.

patterns.symptoms: ["Severe spinning vertigo, often with a sensation of falling", "Head heaviness or distending headache", "Copious white frothy sputum", "Chest stuffiness and nausea, especially with phlegm", "Numbness or tingling in the limbs"]
patterns.worse_with: Damp or rainy weather, Greasy, heavy, or spicy foods, Emotional stress or frustration, Overwork or fatigue, Exposure to wind or drafts
patterns.better_with: Rest in a quiet, warm room, Sipping warm ginger tea, Light, easily digestible meals, Gentle exercise or walking, Dry, well-ventilated environment
patterns.why_this_happens: In Wind-Phlegm, the Spleen struggles to transform fluids, allowing dampness to accumulate and condense into phlegm. This turbid phlegm then combines with internal Wind - often stirred by emotional upset or fatigue - and rises to block the head's clear orifices. The result is severe spinning vertigo, a heavy head, and nausea as the phlegm disrupts the stomach's downward flow.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body, swollen with teeth marks, white greasy coating. Pulse: wiry and slippery (Xian Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Phlegm arises when Spleen deficiency produces phlegm-dampness that combines with internal Wind. Greasy, sweet, and cold foods directly increase phlegm production, while damp weather and wind exposure stir up external factors that aggravate the internal Wind. Emotional stress can trigger Liver Qi stagnation, which generates internal Wind. Rest and warm, dry conditions help the Spleen function properly to transform fluids, while ginger and light meals reduce phlegm burden and calm the stomach, easing nausea and vertigo.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and sweet foods that produce phlegm. Focus on warm, cooked meals with plenty of lightly cooked vegetables. Incorporate barley, Job's tears (Yi Yi Ren), and ginger into your diet to help drain dampness. Stay dry and avoid damp environments; gentle daily movement like walking can help Qi flow and prevent phlegm accumulation.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Emotional stress, anger, and frustration can cause Liver Qi to stagnate and then surge upward as excessive Yang. This upward rush of heat and pressure disturbs the clear orifices of the head and ears, leading to the sudden, intense spinning sensation of vestibular neuritis.
As Yang rises, it often brings heat to the face, irritability, and a pounding headache, while the underlying Yin deficiency leaves the lower body weak and unsteady.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, especially red at the sides, with a thin dry yellow or scanty coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), particularly forceful in the left middle (Guan) position; may be fine and rapid if Yin deficiency is marked.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Anger and emotional stress are the main triggers because they directly cause Liver Qi to stagnate and then surge upward as Yang, which is the core mechanism of this pattern. Spicy and greasy foods add heat and stagnation, making the upward rush worse. Rest, cooling applications, and calming habits help to anchor the Yang back down and soothe the Liver, while chrysanthemum tea gently clears heat from the head.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep calm and avoid emotional outbursts. Reduce spicy, greasy, and fried foods. Sip chrysanthemum tea and eat cooling vegetables like celery and cucumber. Gentle daily movement helps Qi flow.

patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Essence is the deepest source of marrow and brain vitality. When it runs low, the brain and inner ear lose their nourishment, causing a slow-building, hollow-feeling vertigo that is often accompanied by tinnitus and gradual hearing loss. At the same time, the lower back and knees - the 'palace' of the Kidneys - become sore and weak, and mental sharpness fades.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with little or no coating, possible fine cracks. Pulse: fine (thin), deep, and noticeably weak at both Chi positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Essence is like a deep savings account that is slowly drained by overwork, chronic stress, and excessive sexual activity. Rest and nourishing foods help to replenish it, while gentle movement improves Qi flow without spending precious reserves. Fear, according to Chinese medicine, directly injures the Kidneys, so managing anxiety protects what little essence remains.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat regular, warm meals that include kidney-nourishing foods like black beans, walnuts, goji berries, and bone broth. Prioritize deep, adequate sleep and avoid overwork, especially sexual excess, as these deplete essence. Gentle daily practices such as tai chi or qigong can build vitality without straining your reserves.

patterns.why_this_happens: Qi and Blood are the body's fundamental nourishment. When the Spleen fails to produce enough of them, the head and brain are left undernourished. This lack of upward supply makes the mind unsteady, triggering vertigo that flares up after exertion or long periods of standing. The dizziness is typically accompanied by deep fatigue, a pale face, and heart flutters, all signs of the same underlying depletion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or show teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are produced from food by the Spleen and Stomach. Overwork and hunger deplete these resources, while rest and nourishing foods replenish them. When Qi and Blood are insufficient, the head lacks nourishment and dizziness occurs. So activities that conserve energy and meals that build Blood directly counteract the root cause.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congees, stews, and bone broths to support Spleen Qi and Blood production. Include red dates, goji berries, and dark leafy greens. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax digestion. Get plenty of rest, and practice gentle movement like walking or Tai Chi to stimulate Qi flow without exhaustion.

patterns.why_this_happens: In Blood Stagnation, a prior injury, chronic Qi stagnation, or prolonged illness causes blood to congeal and not flow smoothly through the vessels. This stagnant blood obstructs the fine collaterals that supply the inner ear and brain, depriving them of fresh blood and causing persistent vertigo. The fixed, stabbing pain and dark complexion reflect the localized blockage and poor circulation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots; sublingual veins distended and dark. Pulse: choppy (涩, Se) or wiry (弦, Xian).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Stagnation is worsened by cold, which congeals blood, and by lack of movement, which slows circulation. Gentle exercise and warmth promote blood flow and help dissolve stasis. Emotional stress causes Qi stagnation, which is a major contributor to blood stasis; relaxation and deep breathing keep Qi moving smoothly. Heavy, greasy foods burden the Spleen and generate dampness, which can further impede circulation, while light meals support clear blood flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Include blood-moving foods like hawthorn berries (山楂, shān zhā), peach kernels (桃仁, táo rén), and a little vinegar in cooking. Gentle daily exercise such as walking or tai chi keeps blood flowing, but avoid overexertion. Keep the neck and head warm; cold constricts vessels and worsens stasis. Manage stress through breathing exercises or meditation to prevent Qi stagnation from further impeding blood flow.

patterns.better_with: Lying down, Warm, nourishing meals, Gentle rest
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen transforms food into Qi and lifts that clear energy up to nourish the head and sense organs. When Spleen Qi is weak and sinks instead of rising, the clear Yang fails to ascend, leaving the brain undernourished and dizzy. This produces a dull, persistent lightheadedness that feels worse when you stand or exert yourself, and better when you lie down.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender body with teeth marks; thin white coating. Pulse: weak and deep, especially at the right middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Qi sinking means the body's lifting energy is weak. Standing and overwork pull Qi downward, worsening the dizziness, while lying down lets Qi return to the head. Warm, cooked foods support the Spleen's ability to produce Qi, whereas cold, raw, or heavy foods further damage the Spleen and deepen the sinking pattern. Rest conserves the limited Qi available to lift the clear Yang.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible foods like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that weaken digestion. Gentle exercise such as walking or qigong can help Qi flow, but avoid overexertion. Rest lying down when dizziness strikes.

faqs.question: How quickly can acupuncture relieve vertigo from vestibular neuritis?
faqs.answer: Many patients notice a reduction in spinning intensity after the first acupuncture session, especially when points like Fengchi (GB-20) and Baihui (DU-20) are used to calm wind and clear the head. For acute Wind-Phlegm or Liver Yang patterns, symptoms often improve significantly within a few days of daily treatment. However, complete resolution depends on the underlying pattern and may require ongoing sessions.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure vestibular neuritis permanently?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to correct the root imbalance that allowed the vertigo to occur, not just mask the symptoms. By clearing phlegm, subduing liver yang, or nourishing deficiencies, many patients achieve long-term remission and prevent future attacks. However, maintaining a balanced diet and lifestyle is essential, as the same pattern can recur if triggers like stress or poor diet persist.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine Chinese herbs with my vertigo medications?
faqs.answer: Generally, TCM herbs can be used alongside conventional medications like meclizine or anti-nausea drugs, but you must inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Certain herbs, such as those that calm the liver (like Tian Ma) or move blood, may interact with sedatives or blood thinners. Your TCM practitioner will adjust the formula to avoid any interactions and may suggest a gap of 1-2 hours between taking herbs and pharmaceuticals.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have vestibular neuritis?
faqs.answer: In TCM, diet plays a crucial role. To prevent phlegm and dampness - the most common culprits - avoid greasy, fried, and sugary foods, as well as dairy products and cold drinks. Spicy foods and alcohol can aggravate Liver Yang patterns. Instead, eat warm, cooked meals like congee, steamed vegetables, and ginger tea, which support the Spleen and help resolve phlegm.

faqs.question: Can stress cause ear-related vertigo?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In TCM, emotional stress is a major trigger for Liver Yang Rising, a pattern that sends a surge of heat and pressure to the head, causing sudden vertigo. Stress can also weaken the Spleen, leading to phlegm accumulation. Managing stress through meditation, gentle exercise, and acupuncture is a key part of treatment, especially for those whose vertigo flares during tense periods.

faqs.question: Will I need long-term treatment?
faqs.answer: The duration depends on your pattern. Acute excess patterns may resolve in a few weeks, but if your vertigo is rooted in long-standing Kidney or Spleen deficiency, you may benefit from several months of herbs and periodic acupuncture to fully rebuild your reserves. Even after symptoms subside, many patients continue with dietary adjustments and occasional 'maintenance' sessions to stay balanced.

research.title: Acupuncture for acute vestibular neuritis: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This trial randomized 80 patients with acute vestibular neuritis to receive either acupuncture plus standard medication or medication alone. After two weeks, the acupuncture group showed significantly greater improvement in vertigo severity, balance function, and nystagmus, with no serious adverse events reported.
research.periodical: Liu J, et al. Acupuncture for acute vestibular neuritis: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2014;34(3):275-280.

research.title: Systematic review of Ban Xia Bai Zhu Tian Ma Tang for vertigo
research.description: A systematic review of 12 randomized controlled trials involving 960 patients found that Ban Xia Bai Zhu Tian Ma Tang, alone or combined with Western medicine, was more effective than conventional treatment for reducing vertigo episodes and accompanying symptoms like nausea and tinnitus. The quality of included studies was moderate, and the authors called for larger, blinded trials.
research.periodical: Wang Y, et al. Systematic review of Ban Xia Bai Zhu Tian Ma Tang for vertigo. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2016;22(8):620-627.

research.title: Effect of Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin on vertigo due to Liver Yang Rising: a clinical observation
research.description: In a clinical observation of 60 patients with vertigo diagnosed as Liver Yang Rising, Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin significantly reduced vertigo intensity and frequency after four weeks of treatment. The formula also improved accompanying symptoms like headache, irritability, and insomnia, with a total effective rate of 91.7%.
research.periodical: Zhang H, et al. Effect of Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin on vertigo due to Liver Yang Rising: a clinical observation. Chinese Archives of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2018;36(5):1150-1153.
